title: Linux-style open DRAM compiler on U.S. open PDKs
idea: Borrowed from open-source software turning OS kernels into a commons: a 10-person team builds an OpenRAM-like generator for gain-cell and 1T1C eDRAM macros on the SkyWater 130 nm and GlobalFoundries 180 nm open PDKs, emitting layout, sense amps, refresh controller and characterization so any ASIC team embeds MBs of dense memory instead of buying discrete DRAM.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: moves some IoT, edge and defense demand off commodity DRAM onto memory made in U.S. foundries, at ~2-3x SRAM density.

title: 3D-NAND toolset builds channel-hole gain cells with no EUV
idea: Ideal: density from tier count with tools already paid for. Closest: in a NAND-style oxide/word-plate stack, each channel hole holds two concentric ALD oxide-semiconductor devices per tier: an outer write channel charging an isolated metal ring, and an inner read channel gated by that ring, so every tier crossing is a capacitorless 2T gain cell built with the 3D NAND etch, ALD and staircase flow.
why: Facts 2 and 4: 100+ tiers at DUV pitch in existing NAND fabs with no capacitor and no EUV; bit cost could follow NAND-like layer economics if speed and retention hold.

title: Buy bankrupt DRAM makers' patent portfolios to arm a U.S. entrant
idea: Qimonda's buried-wordline and 4F2 vertical-channel work, plus Elpida, Z-RAM, T-RAM and Kilopass portfolios, ended up with patent-assertion entities or in drawers after failure. A U.S. entrant (or a DOE-backed pool) buys or exclusively licenses them to gain freedom to operate for buried-wordline, vertical-channel and capacitorless designs on a low-EUV older node.
why: U.S. manufacturability and entry barrier: removes the litigation and royalty stack that blocks new fabs; buys ~20 years of process R&D for well under $1B, shortening time-to-first-wafer by years.

title: Silver-catalyzed chemical etching makes vertical channel pillars in a wet bench
idea: Effect: metal-assisted chemical etching. A Ag mesh templated by block copolymer sits on Si; in HF/H2O2 the catalyst sinks straight down by local oxidation and dissolution, carving 10-15 nm pillars at AR >50:1 at room temperature with no plasma damage. Ag is stripped in nitric acid and residues are gettered. $1M covers wet benches, TXRF/SIMS contamination checks and 4F2 vertical-transistor test arrays.
why: Fact 4: a ~$100k wet bench replaces $8-15M HAR Si plasma etchers for 4F2 DRAM, and damage-free sidewalls may also shrink the leakage tail.

title: Closed-loop helium: reverse from venting to recapturing
idea: Rearrange the gas flow: put helium recapture, purification and recompression skids on every etch, implant and backside-cooling tool, and switch backside cooling to H2/N2 mixes where the thermal budget allows.
why: Cuts helium purchases ~80-90% while Qatar supply is offline and removes a risk of fab shutdown.

title: Weather-balloon swap: hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in chucks
idea: Borrowed from weather services that fly hydrogen instead of scarce helium: H2 conducts heat about as well as or better than He, so a small team builds a retrofit gas panel feeding 5-20 Torr electrolytic H2 to electrostatic-chuck backside cooling, with N2 sheath, ppm leak sensing and interlocks, qualifying tool by tool.
why: Scarce resource: backside cooling is a top fab helium use and ~30% of helium supply is offline since March 2026; H2 diffusion into devices and safety qualification are the risks.

title: Helium-free wafer backside cooling for a helium-blockade fab
idea: Edge case: Qatar's helium offline since March 2026. Replace helium backside gas in etch/CVD electrostatic chucks with hydrogen-argon mixes or compliant solid thermal-interface chuck surfaces, and switch leak detection to hydrogen-tracer sniffers.
why: Scarce resource: removes the main helium dependence of a DRAM fab with minor recipe retuning; avoids shutdowns.

title: Fab helium recapture loops, fixing why 1990s recovery was abandoned
idea: Earlier fab helium-recovery efforts were abandoned once helium got cheap. With Qatar offline, add membrane/cryogenic recapture skids on every etch and CVD tool's backside-cooling and purge lines with a site liquefier, switch non-critical purges to argon, and use contracts that reward recaptured volume.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): 80-90% recovery cuts fab helium purchases ~5-10x and protects output from supply shocks.

title: He: helium-free fab using hydrogen backside cooling and recapture
idea: Replace He as electrostatic-chuck backside gas with H2 (similar thermal conductivity) or Ne, switch leak checks to H2/N2 forming-gas sniffers, and recover residual He from tool exhaust with membranes, decoupling uptime from Qatari supply.
why: Resource chokepoint: Qatar's ~30% helium is offline and etch/deposition tools idle without it; this keeps capital tools productive.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric 3R-MoS2 channel as a refresh-free 1T cell
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: store the bit as the stacking order (AB vs BA) of a wafer-scale CVD-grown bilayer 3R-MoS2 channel; a gate pulse slides the layers by one bond length, flipping out-of-plane polarization and shifting threshold voltage, which persists without power and without mobile ionic defects to fatigue.
why: Zero refresh in a 1T cell (~4F2 possible) with no capacitor module; sliding switching breaks no bonds, so endurance could exceed HZO FeFETs, and growth below ~500 C fits any BEOL (facts 2, 3, 4).

title: Puff-pastry lamination: bond-thin-flip cycles double 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Borrowed from croissant dough, which gets 2^n layers by fold-and-roll: build a short 4-tier 3D DRAM block, hybrid-bond two such wafers face to face, thin one down to its tiers, and repeat on the doubled stack, so 4 to 8 to 16 to 32 tiers takes three bonding cycles instead of one 32-tier etch.
why: Fact 2: avoids the deep multi-tier etch and cumulative bow; every cycle reuses the same short process, so capex scales with bonders (~$5M) not high-AR etchers. Compounded bond yield is the risk.

title: Three 60-degree line exposures intersect into honeycomb capacitor holes
idea: Box: Si capacitor charge x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x triple sidewall-image-transfer at 0, 60 and 120 degrees. Three spacer line arrays are stacked as hardmasks and the etch opens only where all three gaps coincide, giving a hexagonal hole lattice at ~18 nm half-pitch from DUV line exposures, self-aligned to active lines set by the 0-degree array.
why: Removes the EUV or LELE hole layer for storage-node contact and capacitor (fact 4), since line/space is far easier than holes for DUV; ~1-2 EUV layers saved; risk is compounded LER and hexagonal hole CD uniformity.

title: Substitute random-access cells with short-loop charge-coupled shift-register memory
idea: Store bits as charge packets in 64-stage CCD loops built only from parallel gate lines (no per-cell contacts, capacitors or access transistors), ideal for SAQP or self-assembled line/space patterning; a read clocks the loop past its single sense node using ~0.3 V three-phase clocks.
why: Constraint: a packet transfer costs ~fJ per stage, ~0.1 pJ/bit versus 5.9 pJ per useful bit; facet: line/space-only lithography, no HAR etch, 2-3 critical masks. Latency (~32-64 ns) and dark-current refresh are the risks.

title: Pharma plate screening: composition-spread capacitor libraries on one wafer
idea: Borrowed from drug discovery, which screens thousands of compounds in parallel plates: co-sputter from three targets to make continuous composition gradients (Ti-Zr-Al-O, Sr-Ti-Nb-O) across one wafer, shadow-mask 10,000 MIM capacitor dots, and auto-probe k, leakage and breakdown overnight with one sputter tool and a probe station.
why: Fact 1: finds k~70 low-leakage dielectrics ~100x faster than one composition per wafer, inside a 10-person budget.

title: O: oxidation volume expansion halves pitch instead of SAQP
idea: Print poly-Si lines at relaxed pitch, then thermally oxidize: SiO2 occupies ~2.2x the volume of the Si consumed, so the growing sidewall oxide narrows each gap by a kinetically controlled amount, producing sub-litho trenches that are filled with the second line set.
why: Replaces spacer deposition/etch loops of SAQP with a 100+-wafer batch furnace step; ~30-50% fewer patterning steps on those layers at a fraction of the tool capital.

title: Stack depreciated-node DRAM wafers instead of buying an EUV node
idea: Ideal: more density with no new tools. Closest: keep fully depreciated DUV-only 1x-nm-class DRAM lines running, thin complete wafers to ~3 um and hybrid-bond 4-8 of them into a monolithic stack with a fine-pitch vertical bus, so bits per footprint come from tier count while every tier runs on paid-off equipment.
why: Fact 4 and capital: depreciation (~55% of wafer cost) falls toward ~15%; 8 tiers at half density = 4x bits per footprint; comparable cost/bit with near-zero new capex and no $15B fab.

title: Selectron-style binary grid stack decodes electrons without transistors
idea: Revive RCA's 1946 Selectron, which steered electrons to one storage eyelet by combinations of voltages on crossed grid bars: stack log2(N) thin perforated electrode sheets over a planar cold cathode so each sheet blocks half the windows and only the coded window passes current to its storage pad. Twenty sheets pick one of ~1M pads with 20 drivers.
why: Periphery and capital (Fact 7): decoding becomes electrostatics in vacuum with log2N wires instead of transistor trees, and the 1-5 um sheets are MEMS laminations from depreciated 150 mm lines; risk is pad density, beam crosstalk and vacuum packaging.

title: DNA nanotechnology: origami placement templates for cell contacts
idea: Borrow from biotech: DUV-pattern only coarse binding sites, let DNA origami tiles (C, H, N, O, P) dock into them by shape-selective placement, each carrying a designed 3-5 nm contact or landing-pad pattern, then transfer it into SiO2 by DNA-mediated vapor HF etching.
why: EUV dependence (fact 4): the finest array features come from molecular self-assembly on a DUV grid; DNA synthesis cost has fallen ~10^6x; zero banned elements.

title: Nanoimprint the periodic array, DUV the periphery: mix-and-match
idea: Exploit that a DRAM mat is a perfect crystal: one e-beam master is replicated into imprint templates that stamp the whole array layer (holes or lines) at 12-16 nm half-pitch per field, while ArF scanners pattern only the irregular periphery.
why: Replaces the most expensive EUV array layers; an imprint tool is ~1/5 the cost and ~1/10 the energy of EUV per layer (Fact 4).

title: Public EUV utility leases scanners per exposed layer to DRAM makers
idea: Box: fab-method axis set to tool ownership. A government-chartered utility owns EUV scanners installed inside participating fabs and bills per exposed wafer-layer at a ~3% cost of capital instead of fab WACC ~10%, with take-or-pay terms moving depreciation risk off DRAM balance sheets during downturns.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4): cheaper capital on ~$200M tools cuts per-wafer litho cost ~30-40% and damps boom-bust capex swings; risk is political.

title: Random cell placement mapped after fabrication by on-die address table
idea: Po: lithography happens after the chip is finished. Form cells by mask-free stochastic self-assembly (e.g., nanowire forests at random positions under a coarse word/bit grid), then at wafer sort electrically discover which crossings form working cells and burn a per-die logical-to-physical map into an on-die translation table, an FTL for geometry.
why: Overlay and litho cost (fact 4): eliminates tight-overlay array layers; trades ~10-20% array overprovision plus a small map SRAM for removing 3-5 critical masks.

title: Fiber-optic soot deposition: fully synthetic silica crucibles
idea: The fiber industry makes 9N silica by flame hydrolysis of SiCl4 (VAD/OVD soot) on a mandrel; deposit soot on a crucible-shaped mandrel and sinter it into a fully synthetic crucible with a crystallization-promoting outer layer for hot strength, made from chlorinated metallurgical silicon instead of mined quartz.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes the Spruce Pine dependency for wafer supply using Si, O, Cl, H only; U.S. fiber makers already run the process.

title: Silicon-flux SiO desorption replaces HF-last cleans before epitaxy
idea: Extreme user: space-qualified MBE lines that clean in vacuum without wet chemistry. Remove native oxide by co-dosing a silicon beam/silane at ~750C so Si + SiO2 leaves as volatile SiO, followed in situ by epitaxy, with no hydrofluoric acid at all.
why: PFAS/process: eliminates HF dips (~20-30 per DRAM flow when combined with vacuum transfer) and their wastewater treatment.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM: no dicing, no packaging
idea: Magnify the die to the whole wafer: one 300 mm wafer becomes one memory module with wafer-level redundancy and a bonded edge connector, skipping dicing, die sort, packaging and module assembly.
why: Back-end capital and test: removes packaging steps and per-die test overhead; one terabyte-class memory per wafer for rack-scale systems.

title: Beaker-anodized alumina provides lithography-free capacitor molds on test wafers
idea: Effect: field-assisted oxide dissolution that self-organizes pores. Sputter 3 um of Al on a transistor test wafer and anodize twice in oxalic or sulfuric acid to grow hexagonal pores at 40-60 nm pitch and AR >60:1 with zero litho; a shallow imprinted pre-texture registers pores to cells, then ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN. Budget: ~$60k electrochemical stations, ~$500k ALD and university fab time, plus the team.
why: Facts 1 and 4: HAR capacitor molds without capacitor-layer litho or HAR plasma etch, the two costliest tools in the module; validates 5 fF cells for under $1M.

title: Fe: magnetically chained magnetite nanoparticles as wordline etch masks
idea: Spin a monodisperse Fe3O4 nanoparticle ink into coarse DUV guide trenches, apply an in-plane magnetic field so particles chain into parallel lines with spacing set by dipole repulsion, then sinter into an iron-oxide etch mask that strips in dilute acid.
why: Litho capital: field-directed assembly substitutes for SADP/SAQP on periodic array lines; each avoided multipatterning loop saves ~4-8 steps and an EUV pass. Defectivity is the risk.

title: Print memory directly on package substrate panels
idea: Magnify memory placement onto 510x515 mm organic package panels: inkjet-print oxide gain-cell arrays beside the processor footprint during panel-level packaging, so memory and package are made in one line.
why: Data movement and capital: millimeters from the compute die, no separate memory wafer, and it uses existing panel-packaging lines.

title: Precursor cryo-trap recovery returns hafnium and ruthenium to suppliers
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: ALD uses only ~1-10% of its metal-organic precursor, so fit each ALD/CVD exhaust with a cold trap or adsorbent cartridge that captures unreacted Hf, Zr, Ru and Mo compounds, shipped back to the supplier for re-purification in a closed loop.
why: 50-80% metal recovery lowers precursor cost and Ru supply risk and lightens abatement load (scarce resource, cost).

title: Ca: dry lime beds turn fab fluorine into resaleable fluorspar
idea: Replace water-fed local wet scrubbers on etch/CVD exhaust with a plasma abatement front end plus heated CaO/Ca(OH)2 granular beds that capture HF and fluorine as CaF2, sold back to HF producers as synthetic fluorspar.
why: Water: wet scrubbers are ~5-10% of fab water and drop to ~0; it also closes the loop on fluorspar, a critical mineral.

title: Reusable porous-silicon seed wafers slash crucible-quartz demand
idea: Worse: consume one Czochralski crystal slice, and its share of a Spruce Pine crucible, per wafer. Flip: grow a 20-50 um epitaxial device layer on a porous-Si release layer, transfer it to a cheap carrier or the bonded periphery wafer, and reuse the seed wafer 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resource: high-purity quartz crucible use per wafer falls 90%+ and substrate cost drops.

title: Certified PFAS-free 'clean silicon' DRAM earns EU and defense premiums
idea: Extreme user: EU buyers and 30-year industrial programs facing PFAS restrictions. Create an audited PFAS-free DRAM certification tied to CHIPS-style incentives and procurement preferences, so a fluorine-free U.S. line earns price premiums and guaranteed volume.
why: Capital/U.S. manufacturing: turns a regulatory cost into a differentiator; guaranteed offtake lowers the cost of capital for new U.S. capacity.

title: Double-rate capacitor etch accepting rare not-open holes
idea: Combine high-power, high-rate HAR etch recipes with error tolerance: capacitor-hole etch rate is pushed ~2x with higher bias and fewer passivation cycles, and the resulting ~0.5-1% not-open or twisted holes become dead cells logged as erasures at sort.
why: HAR capacitor etch chambers are among the largest DRAM capex items, and 2x rate halves the fleet, worth $1B+ in a large fab (facts 1, 4).

title: Abacus beads: bistable NEMS cells made in DLP-style MEMS fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'abacus' (beads flip between two stable sides) -> each bit is a nanoscale torsion paddle latched in one of two tilted states by electrostatic hold and stiction-free landing tips, the way TI's DLP micromirror is, read capacitively. It is built by sacrificial-release processing in existing U.S. 200 mm MEMS fabs.
why: Non-volatile and immune to radiation. DMD hinges show >1e12 flips, so endurance is effectively unlimited, and the cells use only Al/oxide/amorphous Si and mature U.S. tools, with no EUV or scarce elements. Risk: scaling the pitch to ~100 nm.

title: Area-selective deposition grows landing pads without a mask
idea: Worse: add a litho-plus-etch layer with tight overlay for every contact and landing pad. Flip: SAM inhibitors block nucleation on dielectric, so ALD/CVD metal grows only on the exposed plug tops. This builds self-aligned landing pads and contacts and removes 2-3 critical litho layers along with their overlay budgets.
why: Masks/EUV (fact 4): 2-3 fewer critical layers (~5-8% wafer cost) and higher overlay-limited yield.

title: Expire-and-regenerate pages: let cells decay, recompute on miss
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: disable refresh entirely; each DRAM page carries a write timestamp, and any page older than its guaranteed retention counts as discarded, so reading it traps to the runtime, which regenerates the data from source (re-decompress weights from flash, recompute activations from checkpoints, refetch KV from a cheaper tier).
why: Zero refresh power; because regeneration is rare for hot data, the fab can target ~10 ms retention instead of 64 ms, cutting required Cs ~3x and with it capacitor height, etch time and support masks (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: Masks with printable defects accepted as fixed erasure addresses
idea: Combine reticle defect maps with on-die bad-cell tables. A printable mask defect repeats at the same array address in every die, so masks with tens of array-region defects can skip repair and actinic re-inspection, and those addresses are preloaded as known erasures in every die's code layer.
why: EUV blanks, defect repair and actinic inspection are a chokepoint at $1M+ per mask, and known erasures cost half the code budget of random errors (fact 4).

title: Interference-printed array: the light itself is the mask
idea: Reverse the role of mask and light: print the periodic cell array with maskless two- or four-beam 193 nm immersion interference lithography (~40 nm pitch, shrunk by one spacer step), and use only a cheap KrF trim exposure to cut array edges.
why: No EUV and no critical reticle for array layers; interference tools are simpler and cheaper than scanners, cutting array litho capex ~50%.

title: Wafers stay put; process heads travel like print heads
idea: Inverts 'wafers travel between tools'. Clamp each wafer once on a precision carrier for its whole front end; spatial-ALD, atmospheric-plasma etch and DUV/imprint heads sweep over a moving row of carriers like a printing press, so chucking, alignment reference and load-lock overhead are paid once.
why: Removes ~30-40% of non-productive tool time (pump-down, transfer, re-chuck, re-align) and most automated material handling; ~20% less capital per wafer start (fact 4).

title: Vacuum-gap floating gate: field-emission writes, no oxide to wear
idea: TRIZ #39 Inert atmosphere (vacuum): replace a floating gate's tunnel oxide with a sealed ~3-4 nm vacuum gap formed by sacrificial-layer release; writes use Fowler-Nordheim field emission across vacuum at a few volts, and with no dielectric there are no traps to generate, while the ~4.5 eV vacuum barrier keeps charge non-volatile.
why: Zero refresh with endurance no longer oxide-limited; a planar 1T cell with no HAR capacitor, using MEMS-style release and sealing already common in U.S. MEMS fabs (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: Vacuum-channel nano-triode as a leakage-free DRAM access switch
idea: Revive the vacuum tube at 50 nm: replace the access transistor with a vacuum-channel triode whose emitter tip and collector are separated by a ~30 nm sealed vacuum gap made by an undercut etch and gated by a surrounding electrode. A vacuum gap has no junction or GIDL path, so the capacitor leaks only through its dielectric.
why: Facts 3 and 10: off-state leakage below 1e-18 A would remove refresh (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) with ~3 masks for undercut and seal. Risks are 5-10 V emission voltage, tip wear and hermetic sealing at DRAM pitch.

title: Hydrogen backside gas replaces helium for wafer cooling in etch chucks
idea: Effect: gas-gap thermal conduction, set by molecular speed and the accommodation coefficient. H2 carries heat about as well as or better than He at the same low pressure, so retrofit a refurbished etch chamber's electrostatic chuck with a low-pressure H2 backside line, leak detection and N2-diluted exhaust, then qualify wafer-temperature uniformity. $1M covers the chamber and 24 months of tests.
why: Helium chokepoint: Qatar's ~30% of supply has been offline since March 2026, and backside cooling is a major fab helium use; H2 can be made on site by electrolysis.

title: Eliminate two EUV contact layers: self-aligned selective-epi bitline contacts and pads
idea: Grow bitline contacts and storage landing pads by selective Si/SiGe epitaxy only on exposed active silicon between spacer-defined lines, so they self-align to active areas instead of being printed with EUV contact masks. Output is an ordinary DDR5/HBM core die.
why: Fact 4: removes the two most overlay-critical EUV layers of current flows; self-aligned contacts tolerate DUV-grade overlay.

title: Regulated-utility fab shells depreciated over thirty years
idea: Split the fab's timescales: buildings, utilities and UPW plants (~40% of capex) become a regulated-utility asset with 30-year recovery and a capped return, leasing space to U.S. DRAM makers whose tools stay on short cycles.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (Fact 4); stretching the slow-aging 40% cuts wafer cost ~10-15% and lowers entry capital.

title: Hydrogen-ion projection exposes straight capacitor holes, no plasma etch
idea: Revive the 1990s-2000s European ion projection lithography, which pushed helium ions through stencil masks, using protons from a hydrogen source instead: 100-200 keV protons cross ~2 um of resist with almost no lateral scatter, so stencil projection exposes capacitor holes at AR >100 directly in a thick resist mold that ALD then fills.
why: Fact 1 under the constraint: aspect ratio is set by proton range rather than plasma etch, and no helium source is used; exposure plus development replaces the hardest etch. Risks are stencil heating and resist sensitivity.

title: One accelerator, many printers: shared U.S. free-electron-laser EUV
idea: Jump the light source from tool scale to building scale: one U.S.-built energy-recovery free-electron laser (national-lab heritage) feeds multi-kW EUV through beamlines to 10-20 simple exposure stations that print only the periodic array by reflective interference, avoiding imported projection optics.
why: EUV power per station up 5-10x at lower $/W and breaks the single-supplier scanner chokepoint for array layers.

title: Continuous Czochralski growth stretches each Spruce Pine quartz crucible
idea: Continuous Czochralski (CCZ) was tried in the 1980s-90s and dropped as batch CZ improved. Feed polysilicon granules continuously into a double crucible so one high-purity quartz crucible grows 5-8 DRAM-grade 300 mm ingots instead of one, with steadier oxygen content for retention uniformity.
why: Spruce Pine (>80%) crucible chokepoint: quartz per wafer down 5-8x; slight retention-tail improvement from uniform oxygen.

title: Cochlear ramp etch exposes every tier's contact in one step
idea: The cochlea maps frequency to position along a tapered duct; print a grayscale, thickness-tapered hardmask wedge once and ion-mill it together with the stack so the slope transfers into the tiers, opening each tier's wordline as a stripe at its own lateral position. One exposure and one etch replace the 30-100 resist-trim cycles of a staircase.
why: Staircases and tier contacts take ~15-20% of 3D memory cost and grow with tier count; a one-shot ramp flattens that, so 150+ tier DRAM (~10x bits/mm2) keeps near-planar contact cost (fact 2).

title: Temporary-tattoo decal: freestanding perovskite membranes as capacitor dielectric
idea: A child applies a temporary tattoo. A materials supplier grows single-crystal SrTiO3 or BaTiO3 on a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 sacrificial layer; dissolving that layer frees the membrane, which the memory fab laminates like a decal onto planar stacked-tier capacitors and bonds at <=300 C.
why: Bulk-like k >100-300 gives ~5 fF in ~0.03 um2 planar footprints in stacked-tier cells, skipping high-AR pillars (fact 1) while the memory fab stays <=400 C. High risk: wafer-scale membrane handling, cracking, patterning.

title: One scaffold printed, then every later layer self-aligns
idea: Po: lithography stops at the first layer. Print a single sacrificial lattice scaffold, then form word lines, bit lines, contacts and capacitor landing pads by successive spacer, selective-etch and selective-deposition steps referenced to it, so no later layer needs overlay.
why: Overlay budget and mask count (fact 4): critical masks from ~5-7 EUV to ~1-2; removes overlay-limited yield loss at F~12 nm.

title: Cl: ClF3 vapor carves 3D-DRAM lateral recesses dry
idea: Use low-temperature ClF3 gas-phase etching, which removes SiGe with very high selectivity to Si, oxide and nitride, to cut lateral recesses across 26-100 tiers in one batch vacuum step instead of wet selective etch and long rinses.
why: Fact 2 plus water: deep-slit wet etches need long rinses and suffer stiction; dry recess cuts that module's water ~100% and enables taller stacks.

title: Material-contrast self-alignment lets each layer inherit the one below
idea: Ideal: one lithography step for the whole cell stack. Closest: after the active area is defined, each later layer (wordline cap, bitline, storage contact) is placed by selective deposition and selective etch chemistries keyed to the material contrast of the layer beneath, so only line-cut masks remain.
why: Fact 4: critical masks per cell ~7 to ~3, zero edge-placement error between inherited layers, ~50% less EUV dependence.

title: Vacuum-linked cluster runs the whole capacitor module airlessly
idea: Combine the cluster-tool concept with the full capacitor module (mold deposition, HAR etch, dry mold removal, electrode ALD, high-k ALD, top plate) on one vacuum transfer backbone. Wafers never see air, wet cleans or FOUP queues inside the module.
why: Removes ~5 wet cleans and their tools, eliminates native-oxide and queue-time losses, and shrinks the module's cleanroom footprint ~40% (capital intensity, water use).

title: Rice-husk and diatomite biosilica makes Spruce-Pine-free quartz crucibles
idea: Plants and diatoms concentrate amorphous silica; acid-leach rice-husk ash or diatomite, chlorinate to volatilize metals, fuse to 5N+ synthetic silica and slip-cast Czochralski crucibles with a synthetic inner liner.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint using US rice-belt and diatomite feedstock in the hundreds of kt per year.

title: Statistical capacitors: unaligned anodic-alumina pores caught by oversized pads
idea: Constraint: no lithography and no plasma etch for the capacitor mold. Anodize a deposited aluminum film into self-ordered ~30 nm-pitch pores (AR >100 for free), deliberately unaligned to the cells; each oversized landing pad catches 3-5 pores, pores straddling gaps are sealed by a selective ALD cap, and the per-cell capacitance spread is trimmed out at test.
why: Facts 1 and 4: swaps the hardest high-AR cryo-etch and its mask for a wet bath; AR 100-200 gives ~1.5x Cs; capacitor-module capex -60-70%.

title: Mature U.S. foundry periphery wafers hybrid-bonded under array-only wafers
idea: Combine Xtacking-style wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with idle U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundry capacity. The DRAM wafer carries only cells, bitline sense amps and wordline drivers; decoders, I/O, DLL, charge pumps and test logic are made on mature logic wafers and bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7). The array wafer becomes nearly all cells and drops ~8-12 HKMG periphery masks, and depreciated U.S. fabs supply half the silicon, so array-fab wafer starts per bit fall ~25-35%.

title: Maskless interference lithography for perfectly periodic array layers
idea: Po: the pattern needs no mask. Because the cell array is a perfect lattice, expose array layers with multi-beam 193 nm interference that writes line/space or hexagonal hole lattices over a whole field with huge depth of focus, using a conventional scanner only to block out periphery.
why: Litho capex and EUV dependence (fact 4): interference exposure heads cost ~1/10 of a scanner and need no reticle; with pitch splitting they replace EUV for array layers.

title: Escalator: continuous flow-line DRAM array fab instead of job shop
idea: Random stimulus 'escalator' (constant flow, no waiting) -> an array-only fab is laid out as a process-ordered linear line, with tools sized to takt time and vacuum or overhead transfer straight between steps. Wafers flow like an escalator rather than queueing in a randomized job shop.
why: Capital and time: DRAM cycle time is 60-90 days, mostly queueing. A flow line could cut it to ~20-25 days, reducing WIP inventory, working capital and the time from capex to revenue for a new U.S. entrant.

title: Prospector without Spruce Pine: reusable crucibles with continuous Czochralski
idea: A prospector cut off from the one quartz mine refuses to scrap a crucible per ingot. Grow DRAM-grade silicon by continuous Czochralski with granular-poly feeding in a long-life crucible: synthetic sol-gel silica made from fumed silica (any sand plus chlorination) inside a reusable silicon-nitride-coated graphite susceptor, pulling 5-10 ingots per crucible.
why: Cuts high-purity quartz per wafer ~5-10x and escapes >80% single-site supply; continuous CZ also evens out resistivity and oxygen. Risk: oxygen and contamination control for retention-sensitive DRAM.

title: Grow capacitor pillars bottom-up instead of etching 70:1 holes
idea: Invert the length-scale problem: rather than etching 1.5 um-deep holes, grow vertical Si nanowires from CMOS-compatible catalyst dots (Al or Cu-silicide) placed on the capacitor lattice sites, then wrap them in ZrO2/HfO2 and a top electrode; aspect ratio becomes a function of growth time, not etch physics.
why: Breaks the AR 60-75:1 etch wall (Fact 1): AR ~150:1 for Cs >8 fF without cryogenic etch tools, removing the single costliest etch step.

title: Parallel MEMS tips write atom-precise imprint masters
idea: First principle: the resolution limit is one surface atom, which STM hydrogen-depassivation lithography reaches; it is slow, but a master only has to be written once. A 10,000-tip MEMS array writes a DRAM array master on H-terminated Si with ~1 nm edge roughness, selective ALD converts it to a hard template, and it is cloned into thousands of imprint working templates.
why: Mask cost and resolution (fact 4): masters with no stochastic edge roughness let imprint go below 10 nm half-pitch; master cost is spread over ~10^6 wafers.

title: Transient-electronics water-soluble GeO2 sacrificial layers replace HF releases
idea: Extreme user: dissolvable military and medical 'transient' electronics. Use amorphous GeO2 (water-soluble) or ZnO (dilute acetic acid) as the sacrificial film for capacitor support release, air gaps and 3D-DRAM lateral recesses, dissolving it in water instead of HF.
why: PFAS/process: every HF release step becomes a water rinse with near-infinite selectivity to Si, SiN and metals.

title: Jelly-roll winding: strained membranes self-roll into multi-turn capacitors
idea: Borrow Li-ion jelly-roll winding: deposit a planar TiN/high-k/TiN/high-k ribbon on a strained bilayer over a sacrificial film, open one release edge, and let built-in strain roll each ribbon into a 4-6-turn Swiss-roll capacitor lying in a shallow trench.
why: Fact 1: plate area comes from planar ribbon length that cheap litho defines, giving ~4-6x one cylinder's area with no HAR etch.

title: Phyllotactic offset leaves halve the tier pitch of 3D DRAM
idea: Leaves alternate around a stem so they never shade each other; build the lateral 3D stack from two alternating SiGe compositions (A, B) and etch two interleaved hole sets, the first recessing only A tiers and the second only B tiers, so capacitor 'leaves' of neighbouring tiers sit half a cell offset rather than stacked. Coupling and leaning loads fall, so tier pitch can shrink from ~60 nm to ~30 nm.
why: Two masks serve every tier; doubling tiers per micron of stack lets an 80-tier stack fit where 40 did, reaching ~10x planar bits/mm2 at near-equal wafer cost (fact 2).

title: Ice hotel: platinum-group-free, tungsten-free MTJ stack from abundant elements
idea: Random stimulus 'ice hotel' (built only from local, abundant material) -> a heavy-metal-free STT stack: MnN exchange-bias pinning instead of IrMn or PtMn, a Cr spacer synthetic antiferromagnet instead of Ru, an Fe-rich FeB/MgO free layer, and Mo caps instead of Ta or W.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes Ir, Pt and Ru (PGM chokepoints) and tungsten (China ~80%) from non-volatile MRAM, using only sputter targets sourced in the U.S. and allies, with targets ~30% cheaper.

title: Pay memory subsidies per gigabyte shipped, not per fab dollar
idea: Capex-first support such as Solyndra's loan guarantee failed by funding plants that never reached competitive cost. Restructure U.S. memory support as a production tax credit per Gb of DRAM-class memory shipped from U.S. fabs, decaying over 10 years, with a bonus per Gb made without EUV layers.
why: Capital efficiency and U.S. manufacturability: money flows to whoever reaches volume and low cost, rewards low-EUV processes, and grows U.S. share from 1-2%.

title: Reuse one donor wafer ten times for 3D tiers
idea: Reverse the substrate from consumed to recycled: grow crystalline Si on a porous-Si release layer on a donor wafer, transfer a thin layer to the DRAM stack, then re-polish and re-grow so each Czochralski wafer gives 10+ tiers.
why: Cuts crystal growth and quartz-crucible demand (Spruce Pine choke) per 3D tier ~10x, and lowers cost per tier for 26+ tier 3D DRAM.

title: Dose-coded grayscale exposure defines three depths in one shot
idea: First principle: a mask carries 2D information, but exposure dose is a free third channel. A halftone grayscale reticle plus a resist with linear dose-to-depth contrast prints the buried-wordline trench, bitline-contact and isolation recess as three depth levels in one exposure, and a single etch with ~1:1 resist-to-substrate selectivity transfers all three.
why: Masks and steps (fact 4): 3 litho-etch modules become 1, saving ~2 critical masks and their overlay budget; ~5% lower wafer cost.

title: Eliminate step-and-repeat: whole-wafer single-shot roll nanoimprint
idea: Roll a flexible replica stamp across the full 300 mm wafer in one pass, patterning every die at once in UV-cured resist; distortion is corrected by thermally actuated zones in the stamp frame, mapped against wafer alignment marks.
why: Throughput and capital: one ~$5M imprint station replaces a scanner for array layers at >100 wafers/hour, with no stitching, projection optics or light source.

title: Sand dunes: phase-locked ion-beam ripples as maskless pitch multipliers
idea: Random stimulus 'sand dunes' -> off-normal low-energy ion bombardment self-organizes surface ripples at 15-30 nm wavelength. A coarse 193i grating locks their phase, as graphoepitaxy does, so each DUV period breaks up into 4-6 ordered ripples that serve as a line hardmask, from a blanket exposure.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): a blanket ion-beam step (~$5M tool) replaces SAQP's repeated deposition/etch spacer loops or EUV for line/space array layers.

title: Bioreactor-grown protein crystals as nanoscale etch masks
idea: Jump from fermentation tank to wafer: bacterial S-layer proteins grown in U.S. biomanufacturing plants recrystallize on the wafer as 2D lattices with 10-25 nm periodicity, and metal infiltration hardens them into a mask for the capacitor or contact lattice.
why: A litho-free 10-25 nm periodic template at ag-biotech cost (cents per wafer) removes EUV from 1-2 array layers.

title: Plasmonics nanosphere lithography: floated monolayer masks for capacitor arrays
idea: Borrowed from plasmonics labs, which float colloidal spheres into a close-packed monolayer on water and lift it onto a substrate: float 40 nm monodisperse silica spheres on a Langmuir-Blodgett trough over a wafer with shallow lattice guides, shrink them by plasma, and use them as the etch mask for the hexagonal storage-node array.
why: Fact 4: replaces an EUV layer with a ~$50k trough a small team can run; the honeycomb matches DRAM's capacitor lattice; grain-boundary defects are the high risk.

title: SpaceX rideshare: multi-project shuttle wafers on a DRAM pilot line
idea: Like rideshare launches that carry dozens of satellites, a national DRAM pilot line offers quarterly multi-project shuttle runs: startups and universities buy part of a wafer on a standard access-transistor and periphery flow and drop in their own capacitor or cell module.
why: Capital barrier to new cells: a cell experiment falls from $100M+ for a private line to ~$0.1-1M per shuttle slot, filling the U.S. pipeline of DRAM-class cells.

title: Substitute tester-based burn-in with on-die BIST and contactless wafer test
idea: Embed a programmable march/retention test engine and near-field RF coupling coils in every die so whole wafers are tested in parallel by a wafer-scale wireless tester without probe cards; weak cells are repaired by on-die eFuses during the same pass.
why: DRAM test and burn-in equipment is ~10% of capex and a throughput bottleneck; massively parallel contactless test could cut test cost ~5x and free cleanroom floor.

title: Constellation-style field self-repair replaces hours of DRAM burn-in
idea: Extreme user: satellite constellations that fly tens of thousands of COTS parts and repair in orbit. Ship DRAM with on-die BIST plus repeatable post-package repair of spare rows at every power-up, and screen infant mortality in the field instead of multi-hour high-temperature burn-in.
why: Test capital: burn-in ovens and testers are ~10-15% of DRAM cost; cutting burn-in time ~70% removes a large tester fleet and floor space.

title: Lower-grade crystals from recycled-quartz crucibles, leakers absorbed by codes
idea: Combine cheaper crystal growth (crucibles with thin synthetic liners over recycled or non-Spruce-Pine quartz, several pulls per crucible) with error tolerance. Higher oxygen-precipitate and metal densities lengthen the leakage tail, and the extra retention-weak cells are absorbed within the 1% budget.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint and cuts wafer cost ~20-30% (scarce resource).

title: Kerfless epitaxial wafers: one seed crystal reused fifty times
idea: DRAM uses only the top few microns of a 775 um wafer: grow a 20-50 um epitaxial Si film on a porous-Si release layer atop a reusable seed wafer, lift it off onto a low-cost domestic carrier, and re-polish the seed for ~50 reuses.
why: Cuts Czochralski pulling, quartz crucibles and polysilicon per wafer by ~10-30x; Michigan polysilicon and U.S. epi reactors suffice.

title: Swiss roll: self-rolling strained MIM film forms horizontal 3D DRAM capacitors
idea: Random stimulus 'Swiss roll' -> in lateral 3D DRAM tiers, a planar electrode/high-k/electrode stack with a built-in strain gradient is deposited, its sacrificial underlayer is released, and the stack curls into a multi-turn coil filling the tier cavity. Capacitor area grows 5-10x with only planar deposition.
why: Removes the lateral deep-recess etch that blocks 3D DRAM capacitors (fact 2). It could reach the ~5 fF target in a short footprint, so more tiers fit per height.

title: Nanoimprint guides plus block-copolymer rectification replace EUV array layers
idea: First principle: imprint costs mechanical work, not photons (EUV turns ~0.02% of wall power into dose), but imprint suffers defects, while block copolymers anneal toward their free-energy minimum and heal defective guides. Imprint coarse 2x-pitch guides, then let a high-chi BCP (e.g., PS-b-PDMS) self-assemble to the final ~24 nm pitch, repairing imprint defects before pattern transfer.
why: EUV dependence (fact 4): tool ~$15M vs ~$200M and ~1/50 the power; removes the single-supplier EUV dependence for array layers.

title: Floating-body 1T cells revived for millisecond-lived pipeline buffers
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: rather than fight floating-body retention (why 1T-DRAM failed), embrace it - build SOI or stacked-Si floating-body cells with ~10-100 ms retention and use them only for data overwritten every few ms (pipeline-parallel handoff buffers, double-buffered GEMM tiles, network rings), with refresh logic removed.
why: Zero refresh; the cell is a single transistor with no capacitor module (~25% fewer array steps, no HAR etch) and stacks readily into 3D (facts 2, 3, 4).

title: Short-purge high-k ALD triples throughput, thin-bottom leakers tolerated
idea: Combine aggressive ALD cycle compression (3x shorter precursor exposure and purge in the capacitor ZrO2/Al2O3 stack) with error tolerance. The resulting thin or under-dense dielectric at the bottoms of some deep holes creates ~0.5% leaky cells that the code absorbs.
why: High-k ALD in AR 60-75 holes is slow and needs large tool fleets; 3x throughput cuts that fleet by two-thirds and saves precursor (capital intensity, throughput; fact 1).

title: Self-aligned imprint: all layer masks in one stamp
idea: Minify alignment steps to zero by encoding all layer geometries as stepped heights in one 3D roll-to-roll imprint stamp; successive etch-backs reveal each level, so layers are perfectly registered even on a stretching web.
why: Masks and overlay: 6-8 aligned lithography steps collapse into one imprint, which makes fine pitch possible on flexible substrates.

title: Universal half-finished wafers finished regionally as DDR, LPDDR or HBM
idea: Po: memory is finished at the customer's door. Freeze a common front end through the capacitor module, bank those wafers, and let regional back-end lines apply product-specific metal, TSV and test, so supply swings between DDR, LPDDR and HBM in weeks instead of quarters.
why: Capital efficiency: less capacity mismatch and inventory write-down, ~5-10% more usable bits from the same capex.

title: Newspaper pressman: roll-to-roll gain-cell memory sheets on steel foil
idea: A pressman prints kilometers of paper per hour. Run planarized stainless or Invar foil through a roll-to-roll line of atmospheric spatial-ALD heads (<=250 C), roll-to-roll UV nanoimprint and web plasma etch to build oxide-semiconductor gain-cell sheets, then cut and laminate the sheets into memory slabs.
why: Continuous web processing at meters per minute could cut capex per bit ~10x for capacity memory, with no wafers, crucibles or EUV. High risk: imprint overlay on a moving, stretching web, and particle defects.

title: Rotary spatial ALD at atmospheric pressure
idea: Magnify deposition throughput 10x by spinning wafers under fixed precursor zones separated by gas curtains (spatial ALD) at atmospheric pressure for capacitor high-k and liners, instead of slow pulsed vacuum ALD.
why: Throughput and tool cost: ALD is a bottleneck in capacitor and 3D flows; 10x fewer chambers per wafer start.

title: Solar spatial-ALD conveyor for DRAM capacitor stacks
idea: Borrowed from solar PERC lines, which deposit AlOx by spatial ALD: wafers move under fixed slots of precursor, purge and oxidant at near-atmospheric pressure, so pulses become positions instead of time steps. Adapt a rotary spatial-ALD platen to DRAM ZrO2/Al2O3/TiN capacitor stacks, removing the vacuum purge cycles that dominate cluster-tool time.
why: Facts 1/4: capacitor-stack ALD is among the slowest, most tool-heavy array steps; spatial ALD claims 5-10x throughput per tool and ~3x lower capex per wafer pass, if conformality at AR 60+ holds.

title: Self-ordering anodic alumina templates for capacitor holes
idea: Minify capacitor-hole lithography to zero: anodize a deposited aluminum film so it self-organizes into a hexagonal nanopore lattice (aspect ratio >100), then line pores with electrode and high-k by ALD.
why: Capacitor charge wall and EUV layers: electrochemistry in a beaker replaces the hardest EUV and high-AR etch step; pores naturally reach AR ~115+.

title: Rubber stamp: electroformed nanoimprint stamper families replace EUV for capacitor holes
idea: Random stimulus 'rubber stamp' -> one e-beam-written master for the hexagonal storage-node hole array is copied, the way CD and DVD presses make stamper families, into father/mother/son nickel and quartz daughter templates. Jet-and-flash UV imprint then prints the periodic hole and landing-pad layers, and a 193i scanner handles only the aperiodic periphery.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (fact 4): the most periodic layers are the ones that carry most of the 5-7 EUV passes. Imprint tools cost ~$10-20M versus $200M+ for EUV, so the patterning cost of those layers could fall 3-5x; daughter templates spread the master's cost over millions of wafers.

title: Partially-good dies become full modules through controller remap
idea: Po: the bad dies are good. Stop scrapping DRAM dies with dead banks or exhausted redundancy; bin them by usable fraction, pair 75%-good dies per slot and let a CXL or module controller remap addresses around dead regions.
why: Yield and capital: recovers ~3-8% of wafer output now scrapped, including HBM stack fallout (fact 6), with zero new fab.

title: Food truck: periphery-as-a-service from U.S. mature-node logic fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'food truck' (cook elsewhere, serve on site) -> the array wafer, which carries the EUV and capacitor steps, is made in a lean array-only fab. The CMOS periphery wafer (sense amps, decoders, I/O) is bought from existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundries and hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7) yet needs no DRAM-specific tools. Moving it to depreciated U.S. logic capacity cuts DRAM-fab capex per bit ~30-40% and creates a U.S. supply path without a $15B fab.

title: Coral reef: electrolytic bottom-up superfill replaces CVD tungsten wordlines
idea: Random stimulus 'coral' (structures grown by electrochemical accretion from seawater) -> buried wordlines, bitline contacts and landing pads are filled by additive-driven bottom-up electroplating of Ru or Co on a sub-nm seed, the way copper damascene superfill works. This replaces WF6 CVD tungsten fill.
why: Scarce-resource intensity (tungsten ~80% China) and tool capital: wet plating cells cost a fraction of CVD-W clusters. Ru/Co lines also have lower resistance at <15 nm width, so wordline delay and voltage drop fall ~20-30%.

title: Shower head: atmospheric spatial ALD for high-k and electrodes
idea: Random stimulus 'shower head' -> wafers glide under a gas-bearing head with alternating precursor/purge/oxidant slots at atmospheric pressure, so every pass is one ALD cycle with no pump-down. It replaces vacuum batch and single-wafer ALD for the ZrO2/HfO2 capacitor dielectric and TiN electrodes.
why: Tool capital and throughput: spatial ALD reaches 10-50x the deposition rate with no vacuum hardware. The capacitor module's many ALD steps could need ~3x fewer tools and less floor space.

title: Fingerprint: random self-assembled cells with a per-die learned address map
idea: Random stimulus 'fingerprint' (unique random pattern, identified after the fact) -> only coarse wordline/bitline grids are patterned with relaxed DUV, and storage elements form randomly at crossings from block-copolymer or nanoparticle self-assembly with no registration. A built-in self-test fingerprints each die and writes a remap table, so the controller addresses only crossings that captured a working cell.
why: Removes overlay and critical-litho requirements for the storage node (fact 4). The design accepts ~60-80% site occupancy in exchange for eliminating several EUV/ArFi layers; this trades 20-40% raw area for large capex savings.

title: Velcro: capillary self-alignment for massively parallel die-to-wafer HBM bonding
idea: Random stimulus 'Velcro' (rough placement, self-locking) -> dies are dropped roughly onto hydrophilic bonding sites wetted with a water film, and surface tension pulls each die to sub-micron alignment before direct hybrid bonding. Thousands of dies are placed in parallel instead of one at a time by precision bonders.
why: HBM TSV tax and capital (fact 6): high-accuracy D2W bonders run ~$3-5M each at low throughput. Fluidic placement could raise stacking throughput ~10x and allows yield-sorted known-good dies.

title: Zebra stripes: superlattice edge transfer defines 8 nm bitlines without lithography
idea: Random stimulus 'zebra' -> an ALD/epitaxial superlattice of alternating materials (for example Si/SiGe) is cleaved and polished edge-on, selectively etched, metallized and stamped onto the wafer as a line array (superlattice nanowire pattern transfer). Film thickness, controlled to the angstrom, sets pitch and CD instead of optics.
why: Litho-bound scaling (fact 4): it enables sub-10 nm half-pitch bitline and wordline arrays with no EUV and near-zero CD variation, and the master superlattice is reusable.

title: Fridge magnet: define MTJ bits by ion irradiation, not etching
idea: Random stimulus 'fridge magnet' (stripes magnetized into a continuous sheet) -> the STT-MRAM stack stays continuous, and He+/N+ or oxygen ions implanted through a DUV-patterned mask destroy perpendicular anisotropy and tunnel magnetoresistance in the gaps, isolating bits magnetically without ion-beam etching the stack.
why: Non-volatile MRAM with endurance >1e12. It removes the MTJ etch (sidewall redeposition shorts, the yield killer) and IBE tools, and could cut MTJ pitch from ~90 nm to ~45 nm at DUV, about 4x density.

title: Rice terraces: bevel-polish exposes all tiers for one-mask contacts
idea: Random stimulus 'rice terraces' -> instead of a 3D NAND-style staircase (many trim-etch loops) for a multi-tier ferroelectric or MRAM stack, a tilted-pad CMP or ion-beam bevel cuts a shallow ramp through all tiers at once, and every plate line is contacted on the ramp in a single lithography step.
why: For non-volatile 3D FeRAM and FeFET stacks, it replaces 10-30 staircase litho/trim cycles with one bevel plus one mask, cutting ~5-10% of wafer cost and much of the cycle time.

title: Sugar cube: water-dissolved sacrificial layer transfers epitaxial perovskite ferroelectric
idea: Random stimulus 'sugar cube' (dissolves in water) -> single-crystal BaTiO3 or PZT-class ferroelectric is grown at high temperature on a reusable SrTiO3 donor over a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 layer. Dissolving that layer releases the membrane, which is bonded onto finished CMOS at <300 C.
why: Non-volatile FeRAM with epitaxial-quality films (endurance >1e12, Pr several times HZO). It decouples the high-temperature growth from CMOS, and the donor is reused, so no perovskite-compatible fab is needed.

title: Compass needle: voltage-controlled anisotropy lets one transistor serve many MTJs
idea: Random stimulus 'compass needle' (flipped by a field, no current) -> MTJs written by voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy, with precessional switching at near-zero current. The access transistor no longer needs to be wide, so 8-16 MTJs share one transistor in a 1T-nMTJ string at relaxed 28-40 nm litho.
why: Non-volatile, with high endurance because no large current flows through the barrier. Transistor area per bit falls ~8x, which reaches DRAM-like density on mature U.S. logic nodes without EUV.

title: Stained glass: ferroelectric memory panels from Gen-8.5 display fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'stained glass' (large panes, assembled) -> 1T1C ferroelectric memory with IGZO thin-film transistors and HZO capacitors is made on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass panels in display fabs, then the panels are diced into CXL memory tiles for a capacity tier.
why: Non-volatile, ~1e11+ endurance. Panel area costs ~50-100x less per cm2 than 300 mm silicon, so even at ~1 um cell pitch a panel holds ~600+ GB, and idle LCD capacity becomes memory supply. Weaker on density and latency.

title: Keyboard matrix: selector-free self-rectifying FTJ crosspoint stacks, two masks per layer
idea: Random stimulus 'keyboard matrix' (keys at row/column crossings) -> a ferroelectric tunnel junction (thin HZO with asymmetric electrodes) rectifies by itself, so 4F2 crosspoint decks need only two line masks each. Eight decks are stacked with DUV SAQP, and a DRAM-front cache plus wear-leveling supply effectively unlimited endurance.
why: Non-volatile, with no transistor in the array and only ~2 masks per deck. Bits per mask rise several-fold versus 1T1C, and the design needs zero EUV.

title: Recipe card: open national NV-memory process kit for 200mm fabs
idea: Random stimulus 'recipe card' -> a federally funded lab line publishes a complete, licensable FeRAM/MRAM-on-CMOS process module (recipes, PDK, test and reliability data) designed for 200 mm and 300 mm mature tools. Any U.S. fab can then add a non-volatile memory product.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: it lowers the barrier from billions in development to tens of millions in module tools and spreads NV capacity across ~20 existing U.S. fabs.

title: Venus-probe vacuum-gap switches with film-thickness-defined critical dimensions
idea: Extreme user: 460C Venus landers, where only vacuum electronics survive. Make the access switch a field-emission vacuum nano-gap whose 5 nm gap is set by an ALD sacrificial layer removed late, so the critical dimension comes from film thickness, not lithography, and off-current is near zero.
why: Litho/refresh: critical features become deposition-defined (50-100 nm litho suffices) and retention is very long; could remove EUV from the cell.

title: Planar AlScN ferroelectric capacitor replaces the 70:1 pillar
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite materials: alloying ~25-30% Sc into AlN makes a wurtzite ferroelectric with remanent polarization ~80-110 uC/cm2 (4-5x HZO), so a flat 30x30 nm, ~10 nm-thick AlScN capacitor sputtered on the storage contact switches ~1.5-2 fC, matching a 5 fF pillar's signal, using PVD tools U.S. BAW-filter fabs already run at volume.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh; eliminates the HAR capacitor module (~20-25% of array steps) and its etch capex; endurance (~1e6-1e8 today) must improve or be buffered by an SRAM write cache (facts 1, 3, 4).

title: B: boron-doped diamond anodes close the rinse-water loop
idea: Pass spent rinse water through boron-doped diamond anodes that electrochemically mineralize organics and oxidizable species with no chemical dosing, then electrodeionize and return it to UPW grade at point of use instead of discharging it.
why: Water: raises recycle from ~40-60% to ~95%, cutting net withdrawal ~10x for the remaining wet steps.

title: Bacterial S-layer protein crystals pattern the array at 9 nm
idea: Many bacteria coat themselves in S-layers, 2D protein crystals that recrystallize on surfaces in minutes; engineer a square-lattice S-layer (~9 nm period) with a metal-binding loop, recrystallize it over the array region guided by DUV-printed edge anchors, mineralize the pores into a Pt/Al2O3 hardmask and etch one vertical-channel gain cell per lattice site with self-aligned spacer wordlines.
why: ~80 nm2 per cell vs ~860 nm2 for 6F2 at F=12 nm gives ~10x bits/mm2 with no EUV in the array; the protein costs cents per wafer, so wafer cost stays flat (fact 4).
